problems.stem: A module discussion prompt reads: "Is AI good or bad for the classroom? Post your opinion." Why does this prompt produce thin posts?
options: It is too long for students to read.
It contains no decision to make; students restate a stance with no specific tension to wrestle with.
It mentions AI, which students dislike.
It asks for a post instead of an essay.
problems.explanation: A closed good-or-bad question has no decision in it, so students just restate an opinion.

problems.stem: To make discussion posts grounded rather than just felt, what should the prompt require?
options: One course anchor (such as TPACK or critical edtech studies) and one detail from the case.
problems.explanation: Requiring a course anchor and a case detail forces evidence-based reasoning instead of opinion.

problems.stem: A facilitator drafting a prompt about an AI reading-level rewriter is offered the auto-suggested follow-up "What does everyone think?" What is the defensible move?
options: Accept it, since more responses are always better.
Reject it: it reopens opinion and drops the named tension (access versus shared common text) the prompt was built around.
Let the tool decide whether to add it.
problems.explanation: A generic follow-up reopens opinion instead of pressing the tension, so the facilitator rejects it.

problems.stem: Which addition most increases the chance that students engage one another's reasoning rather than post in isolation?
options: Tell students to make their posts longer.
Require each student to reply to a peer who took the opposite position on the decision.
Ask students to like three other posts.
problems.explanation: Requiring a reply to a peer who chose the opposite call forces students to engage reasoning that differs from their own.
